claim: Advanced brain aging includes structural defects of intracortical myelin that are associated with secondary neuroinflammation.
source: A key feature of advanced brain aging includes structural defects of intracortical myelin that are associated with secondary neuroinflammation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general observation about brain aging.

claim: Forebrain-specific Plp1 mutants exhibited no defects of basic motor-sensory performance at any age tested.
source: Moreover, forebrain-specific Plp1 mutants exhibited no defects of basic motor-sensory performance at any age tested.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral testing data presented in the manuscript, including rotarod, grip strength, and beam balance tests.

claim: Forebrain-specific Plp1 mutants exhibited catatonia-like symptoms.
source: However, with novel behavioral paradigms, we determined catatonia-like symptoms and isolated executive dysfunction in both genders.
evidence: This is supported by bar test data showing extended response times in PLP cKO mice.

claim: Forebrain-specific Plp1 mutants exhibited isolated executive dysfunction in both genders.
source: However, with novel behavioral paradigms, we determined catatonia-like symptoms and isolated executive dysfunction in both genders.
evidence: This is supported by puzzle box, hurdle test, and complex running wheel data.

claim: Loss of myelin integrity has an impact on cortical connectivity and underlies specific defects of executive function.
source: This suggests that loss of myelin integrity has an impact on cortical connectivity and underlies specific defects of executive function.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the behavioral and histological data presented in the study.

claim: Oligodendrocytes synthesize myelin to facilitate rapid impulse conduction of axons and to support their functional integrity.
source: In the central nervous system (CNS), oligodendrocytes synthesize myelin to facilitate rapid impulse conduction of axons and to support their functional integrity (Nave and Werner, 2014; Stassart et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Advanced brain aging in healthy individuals is associated with subtle myelin defects, as first demonstrated by electron microscopy in aged non-human primates.
source: Moreover, advanced brain aging in healthy individuals is associated with subtle myelin defects, as first demonstrated by electron microscopy in aged non-human primates (Peters and Sethares, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Peters and Sethares, 2002.

claim: There is increasing evidence of oligodendrocyte and white matter defects in a range of neuropsychiatric diseases.
source: Indeed, there is increasing evidence of oligodendrocyte and white matter defects in a range of neuropsychiatric diseases (Nave and Ehrenreich, 2014; Zhou et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The X-linked PLP1 gene is highly expressed in oligodendrocytes and encodes a tetraspan membrane protein of CNS myelin (PLP) along with a minor splice isoform, termed DM20.
source: The X-linked gene is highly expressed in oligodendrocytes and encodes a tetraspan membrane protein of CNS myelin (PLP) along with a minor splice isoform, termed DM20 (Jahn et al., 2009; Milner et al., 1985; Nave et al., 1987).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Loss-of-function (null) mutations of PLP1 cause late onset neurodegeneration.
source: At the other end, the mere loss-of-function (null) mutations of PLP1, such as by a genomic deletion or in Plp1 null mice (Klugmann et al., 1997), cause late onset neurodegeneration (Griffiths et al., 1998), modeling spastic paraplegia type 2 (SPG2) in humans (Inoue, 2019; Saugier-Veber et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Plp1 null mice model spastic paraplegia type 2 (SPG2) in humans.
source: At the other end, the mere loss-of-function (null) mutations of PLP1, such as by a genomic deletion or in Plp1 null mice (Klugmann et al., 1997), cause late onset neurodegeneration (Griffiths et al., 1998), modeling spastic paraplegia type 2 (SPG2) in humans (Inoue, 2019; Saugier-Veber et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Oligodendrocytes not only facilitate impulse propagation but also maintain axonal integrity.
source: The isolated loss of axonal integrity in the presence of myelin led to the concept that oligodendrocytes not only facilitate impulse propagation but also maintain the axonal integrity (Griffiths et al., 1998; Nave, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Oligodendrocyte support of axonal integrity includes glycolytic support of axonal energy metabolism.
source: The latter includes glycolytic support of axonal energy metabolism (Fünfschilling et al., 2012; Lee et al., 2012) and most likely other cellular interactions, such as anti-oxidant defense (Mukherjee et al., 2020) via secretion of extracellular vesicles (Frühbeis et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Loss of myelin integrity and axonal degeneration are invariably associated with secondary neuroinflammation.
source: Loss of myelin integrity and axonal degeneration are invariably associated with secondary neuroinflammation (Kassmann et al., 2007; Lappe-Siefke et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Microgliosis causes a unique behavioral phenotype in myelin mutant mice where mice exhibit longer response times when placed on a horizontal bar.
source: Recently, we discovered in different myelin mutant mice that microgliosis causes a unique behavioral phenotype: when mice were placed onto a horizontal bar with their forepaws, wildtype (WT) animals turn away within 0.2 s, whereas these mutants exhibit longer response times.
evidence: This is based on previous research by the authors.

claim: Catatonic signs in myelin mutant mice were completely lost following the targeted pharmacological depletion of microglia.
source: Strikingly, these 'catatonic signs' were completely lost following the targeted pharmacological depletion of microglia (Janova et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Janova et al., 2018.

claim: Plp1 null mice showed defects in the 'puzzle box' paradigm, which measures the escape latency from a brightly lit open space into a shelter via a mechanically blocked entry.
source: In an independent study (Gould et al., 2018), Plp1 null mice showed defects in the 'puzzle box' paradigm, which measures the escape latency from a brightly lit open space into a shelter via a mechanically blocked entry.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Gould et al., 2018.

claim: Successfully overcoming obstacles in the puzzle box is considered an 'executive function'.
source: Successfully overcoming these obstacles is also considered an 'executive function' (Ben Abdallah et al., 2011; Gould et al., 2018; O'Connor et al., 2014; Pease-Raissi and Chan, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Human catatonia and the loss of executive functions may result from defects in the frontal lobes and its underlying white matter.
source: Human catatonia and the loss of executive functions may result from defects in the frontal lobes and its underlying white matter (Arora and Praharaj, 2007; Northoff et al., 2004), but experimental evidence is lacking.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature, but the authors note that experimental evidence is lacking.

claim: EMX1 is a homeobox transcription factor in ventricular zone stem cells of the forebrain, including the neocortex, corpus callosum, and hippocampal formation.
source: EMX1 is a homeobox transcription factor in ventricular zone stem cells of the forebrain, including the neocortex, corpus callosum, and hippocampal formation (Gorski et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Gorski et al., 2002.

claim: Substantial loss of PLP-immunopositive cells was detected in the corpus callosum and in cortical areas of forebrain PLP cKO mice.
source: We detected substantial loss of PLP-immunopositive cells in the corpus callosum and in cortical areas (Figure 1B').
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1B and quantified in Figure 1B'.

claim: Only sparse PLP-immunolabeling was detected in cortical areas, the corpus callosum, and hippocampus of forebrain PLP cKO mice by light-sheet microscopy.
source: Also here, only sparse PLP-immunolabeling was detected in cortical areas, the corpus callosum, and hippocampus.
evidence: This is supported by light-sheet microscopy data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: In the striatum of forebrain PLP cKO mice, there was no considerable reduction of PLP staining.
source: Expectedly, in the striatum which does not belong to the EmxIRESCre recombination territory (Gorski et al., 2002), we did not find a considerable reduction of PLP staining.
evidence: This is supported by light-sheet microscopy data shown in Figure 1C and the citation to Gorski et al., 2002.

claim: The mid- and hindbrain as well as the cerebellum of forebrain PLP cKO mice showed normal PLP labeling, comparable to control brains.
source: Also, the mid- and hindbrain as well as the cerebellum showed normal PLP labeling, comparable to control brains (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by light-sheet microscopy data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: PLP/DM20 was hardly detectable by immunoblots of prefrontal cortical lysates from forebrain PLP cKO mice.
source: Confirming our image-based analysis, PLP/DM20 was hardly detectable by immunoblots of prefrontal cortical lysates (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The abundance of myelin basic protein (MBP) was unchanged in prefrontal cortical lysates from forebrain PLP cKO mice.
source: The abundance of myelin basic protein (MBP), another myelin-specific structural protein (Boggs, 2006; Nawaz et al., 2013), was unchanged (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1D and citations to previous literature.

claim: The abundance of PLP/DM20 in the cerebellum did not differ between forebrain PLP cKO and control genotypes.
source: Using the cerebellum as a control region that lacks Emx-Cre expression, the abundance of PLP/DM20 did, again, not differ between genotypes (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Close inspection of the upper cortical layers in the medial forebrain of PLP cKO mice revealed a loss of MBP+ fibers.
source: While on first sight overall MBP labeling appeared similar between PLP cKO and control animals in both recombined and non-recombined areas (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), close inspection of the upper cortical layers in the medial forebrain of PLP cKO mice revealed a loss of MBP+fibers (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Quantifications confirmed a local loss of myelin profiles in the upper cortical layers of forebrain PLP cKO mice.
source: Quantifications confirmed this local loss of myelin profiles (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Conventional Plp1 null mutant mice that lack PLP expression in all cells show widespread micro- and astrogliosis.
source: Conventional Plp1 null mutant mice that lack PLP expression in all cells show widespread micro- and astrogliosis (de Monasterio-Schrader et al., 2013; Griffiths et al., 1998), presumably triggered by progressive axonopathy and/or oligodendroglial stress signals.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Significant increases in the area immunopositive for IBA1 and GFAP were observed in the corpus callosum of forebrain PLP cKO mice.
source: We observed significant increases in the area immunopositive for IBA1 and GFAP in the corpus callosum as the primary white matter tract targeted by EmxIRESCre but not in the striatum as a non-recombined white matter region.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: No significant increases in the area immunopositive for IBA1 and GFAP were observed in the striatum of forebrain PLP cKO mice.
source: We observed significant increases in the area immunopositive for IBA1 and GFAP in the corpus callosum as the primary white matter tract targeted by EmxIRESCre but not in the striatum as a non-recombined white matter region.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: Cortical areas that were efficiently recombined in EmxIRESCre animals did not show robust gliosis.
source: Surprisingly, cortical areas that were efficiently recombined in EmxIRESCre animals did not show robust gliosis.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: Significant gliosis was observed in forebrain white matter tracts (hippocampal fimbria, corpus callosum) but not the cortical gray matter of forebrain PLP cKO mice.
source: Again, we observed significant gliosis in forebrain white matter tracts (hippocampal fimbria, corpus callosum) but not the cortical gray matter.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: No obvious differences in the extent of gliosis were found between male and female forebrain PLP cKO mice.
source: In this sex-mixed cohort, we did not find obvious differences in the extent of gliosis between male and female forebrain PLP cKO mice (sex indicated by different symbols in bar graphs in Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: In the forebrain of PLP cKO mice, gliosis is largely restricted to the targeted white matter regions.
source: We conclude that in the forebrain of PLP cKO mice gliosis is largely restricted to the targeted white matter regions.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the immunofluorescence and immunohistochemistry data.

claim: Conventional Plp1 null mutant mice develop a secondary axonopathy throughout the CNS.
source: Conventional Plp1 null mutant mice also develop a secondary axonopathy throughout the CNS (Griffiths et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Griffiths et al., 1998.

claim: In forebrain PLP cKO mice, axonopathy was largely restricted to the targeted white matter areas.
source: In forebrain PLP cKO mice this neuropathology was also largely restricted to the targeted white matter areas: We assessed 22-month-old mice by immunohistochemistry and found amyloid precursor protein (APP) immunopositive axonal spheroids in the hippocampal fimbria and corpus callosum (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: A pronounced atrophy of the fimbria and ventricular enlargement was observed in 22-month-old PLP cKO mice.
source: At this age, we also noticed a pronounced atrophy of the fimbria and ventricular enlargement in PLP cKO mice – a common concomitant of neuroinflammation (Lepore et al., 2013; Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2C and a citation to Lepore et al., 2013.

claim: The prefrontal cortex of 22-month-old PLP cKO mice did not exhibit an increase in APP+ axonal spheroids.
source: In contrast, the prefrontal cortex itself did not exhibit an increase in APP+ axonal spheroids in 22 months' PLP cKO mice, the oldest age tested (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Axonal pathology in forebrain PLP cKO mice included some white matter structures outside the Emx1 expression domain, such as fibers in the internal capsule.
source: However, axonal pathology included some white matter structures outside the Emx1 expression domain. We presume these reflect distal axonal projections from neurons in the target region, such as fibers in the internal capsule (Figure 2C').
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2C' and is an inference by the authors.

claim: In contrast to conventional Plp1 null mice, PLP forebrain-specific mutants remained free of motor impairments at any age.
source: In contrast to conventional Plp1 null mice (Griffiths et al., 1998), PLP forebrain-specific mutants remained free of motor impairments at any age.
evidence: This is supported by rotarod data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and a citation to Griffiths et al., 1998.

claim: On the rotarod, the latency to fall did not differ between cKO and control mice at 6 and 17 months of age.
source: On the rotarod, the latency to fall did not differ between cKO and control mice at 6 and 17 months of age, also when quantified separately for males and females (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by rotarod data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: In several behavioral paradigms in which conventional Plp1 null mice were affected, the PLP cKO mice were normal.
source: Interestingly, in several other behavioral paradigms, in which conventional Plp1 null mice were affected (Gould et al., 2018; Petit et al., 2014), the PLP cKO mice were normal; for example, hot plate (pain), beam balance (coordination), motor performance, and olfaction (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3 and Table 1, and citations to Gould et al., 2018 and Petit et al., 2014.

claim: Forebrain PLP cKO mice showed defects in paradigms that measured executive functions.
source: On the other hand, forebrain PLP cKO mice showed and shared defects in paradigms that measured executive functions.
evidence: This is supported by bar test, puzzle box, and hurdle test data.

claim: Adult forebrain PLP cKO mice showed an extended response time in the bar test, which constitutes a 'catatonia-like' feature.
source: Here, adult forebrain PLP cKO mice showed an extended response time, in which the apparent immobility constitutes a 'catatonia-like' feature (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by bar test data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Both female and male groups of forebrain PLP cKO mice showed delayed response times on the bar as early as 3 months for females and 5 months for males.
source: Both female and male groups showed delayed response times on the bar as early as 3 months for females and 5 months for males (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by bar test data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: When assessed at the age of 20 months, both male and female forebrain PLP cKO mice exhibited significant delays in the puzzle box paradigm compared to controls.
source: When assessed at the age of 20 months, both male and female forebrain PLP cKO mice exhibited significant delays compared to controls (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by puzzle box data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: When analyzed at the age of 20 months, male PLP cKO mice required more time to reach the periphery in the hurdle test in two of two trials.
source: While behaving normally at age 6 months, when analyzed at the age of 20 months, male PLP cKO mice required more time to reach the periphery in two of two trials (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by hurdle test data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Female PLP cKO mice displayed a longer delay in the hurdle test at the age of 6 months, but when tested again at 20 months only with a non-significant trend (p=0.08).
source: Female PLP cKO mice displayed the longer delay already at the age of 6 months, but when tested again at 20 months only with a non-significant trend (p=0.08).
evidence: This is supported by hurdle test data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: In subsequent trials of the hurdle test, mutant mice often lost the abnormal delay, which confirms an abnormal executive function rather than an underlying motor impairment.
source: Interestingly, in subsequent trials (i.e. comparing time points T1 and T2 for each age group), mutant mice often lost this abnormal delay, which confirms an abnormal executive function rather than an underlying motor impairment.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the hurdle test data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Both female and male groups of PLP cKO mice at 23 months displayed reduced total running distance and times in the complex running wheel.
source: Both female and male groups displayed reduced total running distance and times (male total time analysis p=0.056) (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: This is supported by complex running wheel data shown in Figure 5B and C.

claim: The maximal and average running velocities in the complex running wheel did not differ between cKO and control groups.
source: Since the maximal and average running velocities did not differ between cKO and control groups (Figure 5D and E), this performance difference likely reflects a reduced drive rather than altered motor learning.
evidence: This is supported by complex running wheel data shown in Figure 5D and E.

claim: The performance difference in the complex running wheel likely reflects a reduced drive rather than altered motor learning.
source: Since the maximal and average running velocities did not differ between cKO and control groups (Figure 5D and E), this performance difference likely reflects a reduced drive rather than altered motor learning.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the complex running wheel data shown in Figure 5D and E.

claim: The reduced performance in the complex running wheel is in accordance with the reduced executive function in the puzzle box and hurdle test.
source: This would be in accordance with the reduced executive function in the puzzle box and hurdle test.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the behavioral data.

claim: The lack of oligodendroglial Plp1 expression was spatially restricted to neocortex, hippocampus, and corpus callosum by targeting Plp1 in ventricular zone stem cells of the embryonic forebrain by usage of EmxIRESCre.
source: We report the generation and behavioral analysis of a novel mouse mutant, in which the lack of oligodendroglial Plp1 expression was spatially restricted to neocortex, hippocampus, and corpus callosum by targeting Plp1 in ventricular zone stem cells of the embryonic forebrain by usage of EmxIRESCre.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental design and histological data.

claim: Forebrain-specific targeting of Plp1 allowed behavioral tests of higher brain functions that rely on motor output, because the myelinating oligodendrocytes in cerebellum and spinal cord were spared.
source: This allowed behavioral tests of higher brain functions that rely on motor output, because the myelinating oligodendrocytes in cerebellum and spinal cord, which contribute to basic motor-sensory functions, were spared.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental design and behavioral data.

claim: Forebrain glutamatergic neurons are derived from the Emx lineage.
source: Forebrain glutamatergic neurons are also derived from the Emx lineage (Gorski et al., 2002) and are therefore Plp1 mutant.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Gorski et al., 2002.

claim: The myelin-specific protein PLP is not required for neuronal functions.
source: However, the myelin-specific protein PLP is not required for neuronal functions, as directly shown by deleting Plp1 in excitatory forebrain neurons with the help of Nex-Cre mice (Lüders et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lüders et al., 2017.

claim: All Plp1 KO-linked phenotypes, including axonal pathology and neuroinflammation, are caused by PLP deletion in oligodendrocytes and not neurons.
source: All Plp1 KO-linked phenotypes, including axonal pathology and neuroinflammation, are caused by PLP deletion in oligodendrocytes and not neurons (Lüders et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lüders et al., 2017.

claim: Phenotypic effects of forebrain-specific PLP cKO mice are caused by PLP-deficient oligodendrocytes.
source: Thus, also phenotypic effects of forebrain-specific PLP cKO mice are caused by PLP-deficient oligodendrocytes.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the citation to Lüders et al., 2017 and the experimental design.

claim: The cardinal features of PLP deficiency are slowly progressive axonopathy in the presence of close to normal amounts of myelin, with ultrastructural features reminiscent of advanced brain aging.
source: The Plp1 gene was chosen as a target, because the cardinal features of PLP deficiency are slowly progressive axonopathy in the presence of close to normal amounts of myelin, with ultrastructural features reminiscent of advanced brain aging (Griffiths et al., 1998; Janova et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Griffiths et al., 1998 and Janova et al., 2018.

claim: The Plp1 null mutation in mice is a genetic model of human SPG2.
source: Moreover, the Plp1 null mutation in mice is a genetic model of human SPG2 (Garbern et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Garbern et al., 2002.

claim: Plp1 null myelin has subtle ultrastructural abnormalities.
source: Plp1 null myelin has been extensively studied in the past and subtle ultrastructural abnormalities have been described (Klugmann et al., 1997; Möbius et al., 2016; Patzig et al., 2016; Rosenbluth et al., 2006; Steyer et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: PLP provides structural stability to compact myelin and stabilizes the architecture of the 'myelinic channel system'.
source: We have shown that PLP, which provides structural stability to compact myelin, also stabilizes the architecture of the 'myelinic channel system' (Steyer et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Steyer et al., 2020.

claim: Conventional Plp1 KO mice exhibit lower ATP levels in axons of the optic nerves compared to controls.
source: We could further show that conventional Plp1 KO mice, which are well myelinated, exhibit lower ATP levels in axons of the optic nerves compared to controls, when analyzed with transgenically expressed metabolic sensors (Trevisiol et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Trevisiol et al., 2020.

claim: Conduction blocks, axonal swellings, and neurodegeneration in Plp1 KO mice are likely caused by perturbed axonal energy metabolism.
source: This makes it likely that conduction blocks, axonal swellings, and neurodegeneration are caused by perturbed axonal energy metabolism (Fünfschilling et al., 2012; Lee et al., 2012; Saab et al., 2016; Trevisiol et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature and is an inference.

claim: Axonal degeneration leads to secondary neuroinflammation.
source: In addition, axonal degeneration leads to secondary neuroinflammation.
evidence: This is based on the data presented in the manuscript and previous literature.

claim: Other myelin mutants, such as Cnp KO mice, exhibit an even earlier onset of axonal pathology that virtually coincides with the onset of gliosis.
source: We note that other myelin mutants, such as Cnp KO mice (Lappe-Siefke et al., 2003), exhibit an even earlier onset of axonal pathology that virtually coincides with the onset of gliosis (Edgar and Nave, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lappe-Siefke et al., 2003 and Edgar and Nave, 2009.

claim: Inflammation in myelinated tracts is a more general response of resident microglia to oligodendrocyte dysfunctions, possibly reflecting the failure to deliver lactate to the axonal compartment and its release into the extracellular space.
source: This raises the possibility that inflammation in myelinated tracts is a more general response of resident microglia to oligodendrocyte dysfunctions, possibly reflecting the failure to deliver lactate to the axonal compartment and its release into the extracellular space.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the data and previous literature.

claim: Secondary neuroinflammation contributes to reversible catatonic signs in myelin mutant mice.
source: It is this secondary neuroinflammation that contributes to reversible catatonic signs in myelin mutant mice (Janova et al., 2018) and that can now be defined as a clinical feature of forebrain-specific white matter disturbance.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Janova et al., 2018 and the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The specific behavioral defects of Plp1 cKO mice could be caused by the moderate decrease of the axonal conduction velocity, the progressive axonopathy, the secondary gliosis, or any combination thereof.
source: Theoretically, the specific behavioral defects of Plp1 cKO mice could be caused by (1) the moderate decrease of the axonal conduction velocity that was previously reported (Gould et al., 2018; Gutiérrez et al., 1995), (2) the progressive axonopathy that is caused by energy deficits and is likely preceded by conduction blocks in fiber tracts that appear morphologically intact (Trevisiol et al., 2020), (3) the secondary gliosis, as also documented for Cnp KO mice (Garcia-Agudo et al., 2019; Janova et al., 2018), another mutant with structural abnormalities of myelin (Lappe-Siefke et al., 2003; Snaidero et al., 2017), or (4) any combination hereof.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the data and previous literature.

claim: The age-dependent increase of symptom severity suggests that the responsible mechanisms include progressive myelin-dependent axonopathy (with conduction blocks) plus neuroinflammation rather than subtle conduction delays.
source: The age-dependent increase of symptom severity suggests that the responsible mechanisms include progressive myelin-dependent axonopathy (with conduction blocks) plus neuroinflammation rather than subtle conduction delays.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the behavioral and histological data.

claim: The 'rescue' of the catatonic signs in Cnp mutant mice by microglial depletion is in agreement with the hypothesis that progressive axonopathy and neuroinflammation are responsible for the behavioral defects.
source: That is in agreement with the 'rescue' of the catatonic signs, which we consider a readout of reduced executive functions, in Cnp mutant mice by microglial depletion (Janova et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Janova et al., 2018 and is an inference.

claim: Reduced conduction velocity by itself has little impact on cortical processing, as shown for auditory signals in shiverer mice.
source: We also note that reduced conduction velocity by itself has little impact on cortical processing, as we have shown for auditory signals in shiverer mice (Moore et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Moore et al., 2019.

claim: The present work uncouples the role of myelinated tracts for basic motor performance and executive functions.
source: With respect to CNS regions, the present work further uncouples the role of myelinated tracts for basic motor performance and executive functions.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the behavioral data.

claim: Conventional PLP KO mice exhibit first behavioral abnormalities at the age of 3 months.
source: Conventional PLP KO mice exhibit first behavioral abnormalities at the age of 3 months (Gould et al., 2018), that is, before the impairment of motor performance that we had initially determined by rotarod experiments (Griffiths et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gould et al., 2018 and Griffiths et al., 1998.

claim: In PLP cKO mice, the forebrain-specific loss of axon-myelin integrity impairs selectively executive functions that require the multimodal integration of cortical processing upstream of any motor output.
source: Here, we show in PLP cKO mice that the forebrain-specific loss of axon-myelin integrity impairs selectively executive functions that require the multimodal integration of cortical processing upstream of any motor output.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the behavioral data.

claim: Motor performance itself was spared at any age tested in PLP cKO mice.
source: Motor performance itself was spared at any age tested.
evidence: This is supported by the behavioral data.

claim: Olfactory and thalamic input as well as emotionally relevant input into (and from) the amygdala should be less affected in forebrain PLP cKOs, which could explain different behaviors of conventional PLP KO mice.
source: Also olfactory and thalamic input as well as emotionally relevant input into (and from) the amygdala should be less affected in forebrain PLP cKOs, which could explain different behaviors of conventional PLP KO mice (Gould et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a speculation based on the experimental design and a citation to Gould et al., 2018.

claim: The principle finding that PLP-dependent processes affecting myelin and axonal integrity in the forebrain cause the impairment of executive functions is relevant to higher brain functions known to be affected across psychiatric diseases.
source: The principle finding that PLP-dependent processes affecting myelin and axonal integrity in the forebrain cause the impairment of executive functions is relevant to higher brain functions known to be affected across psychiatric diseases.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data and its implications.

claim: Experimental male Plpflox/Y*EmxIREScre and female Plpflox/flox*EmxIREScre mice are termed forebrain PLP cKO.
source: We crossbred mice harboring a floxed Plp1 allele (Lüders et al., 2017) with mice expressing Cre recombinase under control of the Emx1 promoter (EmxIRESCre mice; Gorski et al., 2002), yielding experimental male (Plpflox/Y*EmxIREScre) and female (Plpflox/flox*EmxIREScre) mice, termed forebrain PLP cKO in the following, as well as male Plpflox/Y and female Plpflox/flox mice as controls (controls) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: Male Plpflox/Y and female Plpflox/flox mice served as controls.
source: We crossbred mice harboring a floxed Plp1 allele (Lüders et al., 2017) with mice expressing Cre recombinase under control of the Emx1 promoter (EmxIRESCre mice; Gorski et al., 2002), yielding experimental male (Plpflox/Y*EmxIREScre) and female (Plpflox/flox*EmxIREScre) mice, termed forebrain PLP cKO in the following, as well as male Plpflox/Y and female Plpflox/flox mice as controls (controls) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: A ventral-dorsal gradient of PLP-immunopositivity was observed in the corpus callosum with ventral axons that directly overlie the non-recombined striatum having considerable amounts of PLP+ myelin.

claim: Several behavioral alterations reported for conventional Plp1 null mice were absent in forebrain-specific Plp1 mutants.
source: Surprisingly, several behavioral alterations reported for conventional Plp1 null mice (Gould et al., 2018) were absent and even social interactions appeared normal.
